newsitem.title: USA: INSTANT VIEW - US April durable goods rise 1.4 pct.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW - US April durable goods rise 1.4 pct.

text.p: Following are comments from U.S. economists after the Commerce Department reported April order for durable goods rose 1.4 percent compared to a downwardly revised 2.2-percent decline in March.
U.S. economists in a Reuters survey had expected a rise of 1.3 percent in orders for the month.
ALLAN LESLIE, INDEPENDENT ECONOMIST, NEW YORK: "The biggest surprise was that March, last month's data, was revised (downward to 2.2 percent from a 2.6-percent rise originally)."
Leslie was speaking on Reuters Financial Television.

KEVIN FLANAGAN, VICE PRESIDENT AND MONEY MARKET ECONOMIST, DEAN WITTER REYNOLDS INC: "It was in line with expectations -- maybe a little bit better, which is why we're not getting too much of a reaction in early (Treasury market) trading.
"The gains weren't primarily centered in defense and transportation and you could make the case that in the second quarter, corporate spending looks healthy," he added.

MARILYN SCHAJA, MONEY MARKET ECONOMIST, DONALDSON, LUFKIN & JENRETTE SECURITIES CORP: "The numbers are weaker than some people had feared. There wasn't as much of a bounceback as one might have anticipated, given the 2.2-percent drop in March.

"It's hard to know how much impact the auto strikes had. But transportation orders were up; maybe they would have been higher were it not for the strike. Aircraft orders were down. Future plant and equipment spending, excluding transportation and aircraft, have been down.

"Non-defense capital goods, excluding aircraft, have been down, indicating a weakening trend. Even though the consensus was for durable goods orders to be up just 1.4 percent in April, some people had feared a stronger number and that did not materialize," she added.

DAN SETO, SENIOR ECONOMIST, THE NIKKO SECURITIES CO INTERNATIONAL INC: "Aircraft orders have been jumping around quite a bit. We had a big decline in transportation orders last month and they bounced back this time. Excluding transportation, it's more a picture of stability.

"There are so many ways to cut these durable goods numbers. Ex-defense and ex-transportation, there is a slight hint of softness. But I don't consider that the start of a trend. We'll resume growth (in durable goods orders). The big ticket items are always difficult to predict, but overall capital spending will continue to show moderate growth."

JOSEPH DZIWURA, VICE PRESIDENT AND AN ECONOMIST, THE SAKURA BANK LTD: "Overall, when you look at the non-defense capital goods down 1.3 percent ... business investment going forward should be somewhat moderate and I think that is somewhat pleasing to the (Treasury) market."

HUGH JOHNSON, CHIEF INVESTMENT OFFICER, FIRST ALBANY CORP: "Non-defense capital goods orders were down 1.3 percent and they are the most important component of the release; it's one of the 10 components of the index of leading economic indicators and it gives you a better sense of the trend of orders. So, on balance this is a positive report.

"The headlines are not startling and the good news is that non-defense orders were down and that's consistent with the view that the economy may be slowing and may continue to slow. I would say this is encouraging for bonds, encouraging for stocks and encouraging for the (Federal Reserve)."
